pages.text:
*Rule 1 of the Library at the Bottom of the Sea: Every book is a door. Knock gently.*

The trouble with words, Wren Tidewell had decided, was that they would not stay still.

They swam. On the page they looked perfectly ordinary, black and small and lined up in rows like well-behaved children, but the moment she looked straight at them they began to wriggle, like minnows in a tide pool, and by the time she had caught one, three more had darted away.

It was a great pity, because Wren loved stories more than anything in the world.

She lived in Saltmarrow, a small grey harbor town at the edge of a very large sea, where the fishing boats bobbed at the dock and an old white lighthouse stood on the rocks like a chess piece nobody had moved in years. She was ten. She wore a coral-red sweater, dark-blue overalls and a pair of yellow rubber boots that squeaked. And she had heard, by her own careful count, more than four hundred stories, and could tell every one of them back, word for word.
pages.image: The small grey harbor town of Saltmarrow at morning with fishing boats bobbing at a wooden dock and an old white stone lighthouse on the rocks beyond; in the foreground Wren, a ten-year-old girl with short black curls in a coral-red sweater, blue denim overalls and yellow rubber boots, stands on the dock looking out at the sea.

pages.text:
In Room 4, on Monday morning, it was reading-aloud time.

Ms. Alvarez went round the room the way she always did, in a slow circle, and the children read one paragraph each. Ravi Nair went first, because he always did. Ravi read the way a stone skips across water: fast, flat and without a single splash. He finished a whole page before the clock had ticked twelve times, and sat down looking pleased and a little bit lonely, the way he usually did.

Then it was Wren's turn.

She looked at the page. The words began to swim. "The ship sailed into the har..." she said. "The har..." The letters wriggled. Somebody's chair creaked. "The har-bor."

Nobody laughed. That was the worst part. Room 4 was a kind room, and it went quiet in a kind way, which is the quietest sort of quiet there is, and it lasted for as long as it took Wren to read four more sentences.

At the end she put up her hand and said she had a stomachache. She didn't. It was only the quiet.
pages.image: A bright classroom in a small harbor school; Wren, a ten-year-old girl with short black curls in a coral-red sweater and blue denim overalls, sits at a desk holding up her hand with a pained look while her classmates sit quietly, and beside her Ravi, a boy with a side part in a blue-and-white striped shirt, looks down at his book.

pages.text:
After school Wren sat on the end of the ferry dock with her boots swinging over the water, waiting for the last boat of the day. Ravi Nair sat down on the other end, a careful yard away, with his brown canvas satchel on his knees. Ravi and Wren had lived next door to each other for six years without ever quite becoming friends.

"It's really not hard," he said, after a while, in the stiff voice of somebody trying to be kind. "You just read the words. I read forty-one books this summer."

"Forty-one," said Wren.

"Forty-one," said Ravi. "I keep a list."

Wren did not say that she had heard four hundred stories, or that she could still tell him the one about the lighthouse keeper's goat. She did not say that telling a person to "just read the words" was like telling a person to "just swim." She only nodded, and looked at the water, and wondered how a person could read forty-one books and still look so alone doing it.
pages.image: The end of a wooden ferry dock in the late afternoon: Wren, a ten-year-old girl with short black curls, a coral-red sweater, blue denim overalls and yellow rubber boots, sits with her boots dangling over the water, and a careful yard away Ravi, a boy with a side part in a blue-and-white striped shirt and khaki shorts and red sneakers, sits with a brown canvas satchel on his knees.

pages.text:
The last ferry of the day was called the *Gull*, and it was the smallest and most crooked boat in the harbor, white with a blue stripe and a funnel that puffed. Wren's dad was its pilot. His name was Ben Tidewell, and he was a tall, brown, bearded man in a green wool cap, and he knew the tides the way other people know their own front doors.

On the ride home across the bay the *Gull* rocked and the gulls wheeled, and Wren sat in her usual place on the wooden bench by the wheelhouse, and her dad told her a story.

It was about a crab who thought he was a captain and a captain who thought he was a crab. Wren listened with her whole body. She tapped the rhythm of it on her knee. By the time the boat bumped the dock she knew it by heart, every word and every pause, and it was hers forever.

"Dad," she said, "why can I remember everything I hear and nothing I read?"

He thought about it all the way to the mooring rope. "Stories aren't in the words, Wren-bird," he said. "The words are only the boat."
pages.image: The small white ferry Gull with a blue stripe crossing a blue bay with gulls wheeling overhead; at the wheelhouse Ben, a tall man with a short black beard in a green wool cap and navy sweater, smiles down at Wren, a ten-year-old girl with short black curls in a coral-red sweater and yellow rubber boots, who sits on a wooden bench tapping her knee.

pages.text:
That night Wren lay in her attic room under the sloping roof with the window open a crack, listening to the sea.

On the wall beside her bed hung the tide table, a long chart of numbers that her dad updated every month in his slow careful handwriting. High tide, low tide, high tide, low tide, the sea breathing in and out, day after day. Wren knew what every number meant, because he had sung her the rhymes.

Every few seconds the beam of the old lighthouse swept across her ceiling, white and slow and silent.

She lay there and wished, not out loud, because wishes are shy, for one place in the world where words held still. Just one. A place where she could read as slowly as she liked, and nobody would ever go quiet.

Far out beyond the harbor, and far down under all that dark, something enormous and patient turned over in its sleep.
pages.image: Wren, a ten-year-old girl with deep-brown skin and short black curls in pajamas, lies in bed in a cozy attic room with a sloping roof, an open window showing the night sea and a lighthouse beam sweeping across the ceiling, a long tide chart pinned to the wall beside her bed.
